extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature and philosophy (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and interpretation of Montaigne's Essays (translated text, prefaces, and letters), extracting authorial principles about writing, conduct, and judgment found in the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and plainness in autobiographical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The author declares his aim was domestic and private; he wishes to be ‘viewed as I appear in mine own genuine, simple, and ordinary manner, without study and artifice: for it is myself I paint.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid seeking worldly favour with 'borrowed beauties'; present defects and natural form 'to the life'; write honestly so kin and friends may recover 'traits of my conditions and humours.' Anti-pattern: embellishing or fabricating to charm readers rather than to record oneself truthfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim writing at particular, private utility rather than public glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne states he 'proposed to myself no other than a domestic and private end' and dedicated the book to kinsfolk and friends for their particular commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for usefulness to immediate circle over ambitious public acclaim; keep intention modest and personal. Scoring note: work judged more authentic when its motive is private rather than performative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clemency and generosity as superior instruments of conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne argues that when conquest cannot be completed by arms, 'the end has been accomplished by clemency and generosity, excellent lures to draw men particularly towards the just and legitimate side.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice to rulers/commanders: use mercy and generosity to win loyalty; if punishment is to be applied, 'let it be deferred till success has been assured.' Examples given (historical sieges) illustrate how leniency secures lasting allegiance; anti-pattern: immediate harshness that alienates potential supporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be beloved rather than feared
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to kings: desire that 'you may be beloved rather than feared by your people, and believing that your welfare and theirs are of necessity knit together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority on building goodwill and reputation through humane conduct; suffering temporary disorder (e.g., soldier gains) may be preferable to losing 'glorious credit' gained by clemency. Evaluation favors policies that foster affection and long-term stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve affability and frankness in private intercourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne praises a ruler who 'has condescended to take thought for my age, no less than for the desire which I have to see you' and says 'the preservation of your old affability and frankness in private intercourse is entitled to an equal share of praise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing simple, candid behavior in private relations as equally important to public dignity; criterion for judging character: accessibility and unaffectedness in private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple means may achieve the same end (practical pluralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay's central thesis: 'The most usual way of appeasing ... is by submission ... and yet bravery, constancy, and resolution, however quite contrary means, have sometimes served to produce the same effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single correct tactic; assess context and recognise that opposing strategies (submission vs. resolute defiance) can both produce mercy or reconciliation. Use historical examples to justify pluralist practical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour and admirable conduct can induce clemency
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne repeatedly shows through examples that demonstrations of bravery, constancy, or magnanimity often moved victors to pity or admiration and thereby secured mercy (e.g., the three cavaliers at Limoges; Phyton at Reggio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions or framing appeals, emphasize honourable conduct and courage as means to generate respect and leniency. Counterexamples are provided (cases where valour did not avail) to caution against overgeneralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of passions; excessive sorrow is stupefying
rubrics_metrics.description: On sorrow: 'For all passions that suffer themselves to be relished and digested are but moderate: ... deep sorrows are dumb.' Excessive grief stupefies the soul and deprives it of ordinary functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praxis: cultivate firmness; value passions that admit expression and reason. Examples and literary citations illustrate that extreme emotions incapacitate speech and action. Anti-pattern: glorifying prolonged, performative sorrow as wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and self-knowledge: 'do thine own work, and know thyself'
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne endorses the precept to be present with oneself, avoid perpetual anxiety about the future, 'do thine own work,' and 'know what he is, and that which is proper to himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for good living and judgment: focus on immediate duties and authentic capacities; avoid futile overreaching. Recommended as both ethical and pragmatic guidance; quotes Plato, Seneca, and Epicurus as supporting authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish obedience to office from esteem for virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne: 'We owe subjection and obedience to all our kings, whether good or bad, alike, for that has respect unto their office; but as to esteem and affection, these are only due to their virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rulers and officials on two axes: legal/political authority (which merits obedience) vs. moral worth (which merits esteem). Do not conflate duty to office with personal admiration; archival and historical judgment should reflect this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posthumous evaluation of princes as a useful custom
rubrics_metrics.description: He approves of examining princes' actions after their decease: 'They are equals with, if not masters of the laws ... what justice could not inflict upon their persons, 'tis but reason should be executed upon their reputations and the estates of their successors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical and political justice, allow retrospective assessment and correction of reputations and legacies; avoid protecting memory for private obligations at the expense of public justice. Use as a criterion in historiography and collective memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in reporting facts and mixing hearsay with fact for full information
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Governor of Guienne letter Montaigne explicitly mixes 'the more or less probable hearsay of the town with actual matter of fact, that you may be in possession of everything.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When informing a superior or composing a dispatch, be transparent about the reliability of information—label rumours versus confirmed facts and include both to give a comprehensive situational picture. Practical guidance: keep vigilance (gates, funds), report promptly, and state uncertainties.
